subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The point of incipient plasmolysis is reached when:
options: the cell wall ruptures
the protoplast just begins to pull away from the cell wall and pressure potential is zero
the cell is fully turgid with maximum pressure potential
the cell gains maximum water
questions.explain: At incipient plasmolysis the membrane is on the verge of detaching from the wall; the pressure potential is zero, so water potential equals the solute potential.

questions.q: The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide (and fall in pH):
options: Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given partial pressure
Increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left, increasing haemoglobin's affinity
Has no effect on oxygen affinity
questions.explain: Higher CO2 lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve right so more oxygen is unloaded in respiring tissues.

questions.q: A prosthetic group differs from a coenzyme in that a prosthetic group is:
options: always an inorganic metal ion in solution
a permanently and tightly bound non-protein component of the enzyme
a temporarily bound vitamin derivative
the substrate of the reaction
questions.explain: A prosthetic group is permanently bound to the enzyme (e.g. FAD in some dehydrogenases), unlike a coenzyme which associates only transiently.

questions.q: In plant cells, water potential is determined by the equation:
options: Psi = solute potential - pressure potential
Psi = solute potential + pressure potential
Psi = solute potential x pressure potential
Psi = pressure potential - solute potential
questions.explain: Water potential equals the (negative) solute potential plus the (usually positive) pressure potential exerted by the cell wall.

questions.q: The sino-atrial node (SAN) is described as the pacemaker of the heart because it:
options: Prevents the atria and ventricles from contracting together
Receives blood from the vena cava
Initiates waves of excitation that set the basic heart rate
Conducts the impulse to the ventricles after a delay
questions.explain: The SAN spontaneously generates waves of depolarisation that spread across the atria and set the heart's intrinsic rhythm.

questions.q: Why does a single circulatory system (as in fish) deliver blood to the body at a lower pressure than a double system?
options: Fish have no heart
The heart has four chambers in fish
Fish blood is more viscous
Blood passes through the gill capillaries before reaching the body, so pressure drops before systemic delivery
questions.explain: In a single circuit blood loses pressure passing through the gill capillaries, so it reaches the body more slowly than in a double system.

questions.q: Unlike simple diffusion, the rate of facilitated diffusion reaches a plateau at high concentration gradients because:
options: the molecules run out
the transport proteins become saturated, limiting the rate
the membrane denatures
ATP becomes limiting
questions.explain: When all carrier or channel proteins are working at maximum capacity, the number of transport proteins limits the rate, producing a plateau.

questions.q: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is usually measured as the INITIAL rate because:
options: at the start substrate is plentiful and not yet limiting, giving the true maximum rate for those conditions
product inhibits the enzyme immediately
temperature is highest at the start
the enzyme is most denatured at the start
questions.explain: Initial rate is measured before substrate depletion or product accumulation slow the reaction, giving a valid comparison of conditions.

questions.q: Fetal haemoglobin has a dissociation curve to the LEFT of adult haemoglobin because:
options: It must release oxygen more readily to the placenta
It has a higher affinity for oxygen, allowing it to load oxygen from maternal blood at the placenta
It is less saturated at every partial pressure of oxygen
It carries less oxygen overall
questions.explain: A higher oxygen affinity (curve to the left) lets fetal Hb take up oxygen from maternal Hb across the placenta.

questions.q: A waxy cuticle on the upper surface of a leaf is an adaptation that:
options: Allows more carbon dioxide to diffuse inward
Reduces water loss by evaporation through the upper epidermis
Increases the rate of transpiration
Provides the main site of gas exchange
questions.explain: The waterproof waxy cuticle limits evaporative water loss from the leaf surface, conserving water.

questions.q: The fluid-mosaic model describes the cell membrane as:
options: a continuous protein sheet with no lipid
a rigid layer of protein sandwiched between lipid
a single layer of phospholipids
a fluid phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in a mosaic pattern
questions.explain: The model depicts a fluid bilayer in which proteins are scattered like a mosaic and can move laterally within the membrane.

questions.q: Adding solute to pure water causes the water potential to:
options: remain at zero
double
become more positive
become more negative
questions.explain: Solute molecules lower the free energy of water, making the solute (and overall) potential more negative than zero.

questions.q: Beetroot pieces leak red pigment more rapidly when placed in 50% ethanol than in water because ethanol:
options: denatures the pigment so it appears redder
lowers the temperature of the cells
dissolves and disrupts the phospholipid bilayer, increasing membrane permeability
increases the pressure potential of the cells
questions.explain: Organic solvents such as ethanol dissolve membrane lipids and disrupt the bilayer, increasing permeability so the pigment leaks out faster.

questions.q: Bulk transport of large quantities of material out of a cell by vesicles fusing with the membrane is called:
options: facilitated diffusion
endocytosis
osmosis
exocytosis
questions.explain: Exocytosis is the energy-requiring process in which vesicles fuse with the cell-surface membrane to release their contents outside the cell.

questions.q: A glycoprotein on the cell-surface membrane functions mainly as:
options: a channel for water only
a cell-surface receptor or recognition site for cell signalling and identification
an enzyme that synthesises lipids
a source of ATP
questions.explain: Carbohydrate chains on glycoproteins act as recognition markers and receptors for hormones and in cell-to-cell recognition.

questions.q: When investigating the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme rate, why is it important to use a buffer solution?
options: to keep pH constant so that pH does not act as an uncontrolled variable affecting the active site
to act as a competitive inhibitor
to provide additional substrate
to raise the temperature
questions.explain: A buffer maintains constant pH, controlling a variable that would otherwise alter the enzyme's tertiary structure and confound results.

questions.q: The very large surface area of the small intestine for absorption is produced by:
options: Numerous goblet cells secreting mucus
Villi and microvilli on the epithelial cells
A dense capillary network in the submucosa only
A thick muscular wall
questions.explain: Folded villi each covered in microvilli (the brush border) massively increase the absorptive surface area of the ileum.

questions.q: Cholesterol in the cell membrane functions to:
options: catalyse condensation reactions
regulate membrane fluidity and stability by sitting between phospholipids
provide the main hydrophilic channels
transport glucose across the membrane
questions.explain: Cholesterol fits between phospholipid tails, restricting their movement to maintain fluidity and mechanical stability across temperatures.

questions.q: Tissue fluid is formed at the arteriole end of a capillary mainly because:
options: Hydrostatic (blood) pressure exceeds the oncotic pull of plasma proteins, forcing fluid out
Oncotic pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure
Plasma proteins leave the capillary
The low water potential of the blood draws water out
questions.explain: At the arteriole end high hydrostatic pressure outweighs the water potential gradient created by plasma proteins, so fluid is forced out.

questions.q: On a rate-against-substrate-concentration graph, increasing the concentration of a COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: have no effect on the curve
lower the Vmax that can be reached
increase the substrate concentration needed to reach the same rate, but Vmax is still attainable
prevent Vmax ever being reached even at infinite substrate
questions.explain: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by sufficient substrate, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed to approach it.

questions.q: At high substrate concentration with fixed enzyme concentration, the rate of reaction plateaus because:
options: the pH has changed
all active sites are occupied so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor
the substrate is used up
the enzyme has denatured
questions.explain: When substrate is in excess, every active site is continually occupied, so the number of enzyme molecules limits the rate.

questions.q: In the ileum epithelial cell, the sodium-potassium pump that maintains glucose co-transport is located in the:
options: Basolateral membrane facing the blood
Nuclear membrane
Apical (microvillus) membrane facing the lumen
Membrane of the mitochondria
questions.explain: The Na+/K+ pump sits on the basolateral membrane, pumping Na+ into the blood to keep intracellular Na+ low so apical co-transport continues.

questions.q: Active transport is inhibited by a respiratory poison such as cyanide because:
options: it prevents ATP production, removing the energy needed to pump substances against their gradient
it blocks simple diffusion
it increases the concentration gradient
the poison denatures the phospholipid bilayer
questions.explain: Active transport depends on ATP from aerobic respiration; inhibiting respiration removes the energy source, halting the pumping of substances against their gradient.

questions.q: Companion cells are essential to phloem transport because they:
options: Conduct water under tension like xylem vessels
Store starch for the sieve tubes
Provide ATP and actively load sucrose into the sieve tube elements
Contain no organelles, reducing resistance to flow
questions.explain: Companion cells, rich in mitochondria, actively load sucrose into sieve tubes at the source, driving mass flow.

questions.q: During ventricular systole, the atrioventricular valves close because:
options: The semilunar valves are open
Ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure
The ventricles are relaxing and filling
Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
questions.explain: As the ventricles contract their pressure rises above that of the atria, forcing the AV valves shut to prevent backflow.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is mostly transported in the blood as:
options: Carbonic acid in the plasma
Hydrogencarbonate ions formed in red blood cells
Carbaminohaemoglobin
Dissolved CO2 in the plasma
questions.explain: Most CO2 is converted by carbonic anhydrase in red cells to carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogencarbonate ions carried in the plasma.

questions.q: Most tissue fluid is returned to the circulation by the:
options: Combination of osmotic return at the venule end and drainage by the lymphatic system
Arteriole end of the capillary
Active transport across the capillary wall
Venule end of the capillary only, driven by osmosis
questions.explain: Some fluid re-enters at the venule end down a water-potential gradient, and the excess is collected and returned by the lymphatic system.

questions.q: On a Michaelis-Menten curve, the Km value of an enzyme represents the substrate concentration at which:
options: the reaction stops completely
all active sites are denatured
the enzyme concentration is zero
the reaction rate is half of Vmax
questions.explain: Km is the substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate; a low Km indicates a high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.

questions.q: On a graph of reaction rate against temperature for a human enzyme, the rate rises to a peak around 37 C then falls sharply. The sharp fall above 40 C is best explained by:
options: denaturation as bonds maintaining the active site break
a fall in substrate concentration
a continued increase in kinetic energy
an increase in enzyme concentration
questions.explain: Beyond the optimum, excessive vibration breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the tertiary structure, denaturing the active site and sharply reducing activity.

questions.q: In phloem, the mass-flow hypothesis explains translocation as a result of:
options: Active loading of sucrose at the source lowering water potential, drawing in water and raising hydrostatic pressure that drives flow to the sink
Diffusion of sucrose from source to sink
Capillary action in the sieve tubes
Cohesion-tension pulling sap upward
questions.explain: Sucrose loaded at the source lowers water potential so water enters by osmosis, raising pressure and forcing sap toward sinks where sucrose is unloaded.
